entities.name: Wazir Khan Mosque
entities.label: Institution
entities.summary:
Wazir Khan Mosque in Lahore, Pakistan is considered the most ornately decorated mosque in the Mughal Empire, built between 1634 and 1641 CE by Shah Jahan's governor of Lahore, Hakim Ilm ud-din Ansari (known as Wazir Khan). Unlike the massive scale of imperial mosques, Wazir Khan is intimate, jewel-like — its every surface covered in kashi (faience tile work) depicting geometric and floral patterns in brilliant turquoise, green, yellow, and ultramarine, creating what has been called 'the most beautifully decorated mosque in the world.'

The mosque's five-arched façade is covered entirely in Lahori faience tile work in arabesque patterns, Quranic verses, and calligraphic inscriptions — more extensive than any other Mughal building. The four tall, slender minarets frame a courtyard whose every surface — entrance gateway, prayer hall exterior, interior walls — is covered in painted stucco (parchin kari) and tile mosaics. The total effect is unlike any other mosque: precious and intricate rather than monumental.

The mosque remained active but deteriorated significantly during British colonialism, when surrounding bazaar construction narrowed the entrance passage. The 2009 Aga Khan Trust for Culture partnership with the Lahore Conservation Society launched the most comprehensive restoration of a Mughal monument in Pakistan's history, cleaning and repairing the unique faience tile work. Wazir Khan Mosque's detailed tile patterns are now Pakistan's most significant conservation challenge.
